skip_reason: Post-move billing dispute and refund negotiation on a completed job, not a new-business sales conversation. John Jordan's move is already done and paid; he is calling because the final bill came in at roughly twice the auto-booking quote ('now $2,450 is literally twice as much as I've been quoted'). The entire call is Sergio reconstructing the quote history, then negotiating and issuing a refund against the card on file. There is no lead intake, no availability or booking attempt, no differentiator pitch, and no new move being sold — the pricing talk is retroactive adjustment of work already delivered. The 85-point sales scorecard does not apply and this call should not count toward the sales grading average.
top_strength: Sergio resolved a legitimate 2x-overage complaint without defensiveness and then corrected himself against his own interest. He named the root cause honestly rather than defending the quote — '1500 square foot with the elevator on the fifth floor. Needs three guys when the get going and probably set those expectations. At the beginning, the unfortunate part. Is that this expectations for the beginning you were just kinda hit with it last minute.' When the customer tried to settle for less than Sergio's own stated offer, Sergio flagged the math error against himself instead of pocketing it: 'I'm gonna be honest I said $760 and that's like exceeding what you were asking.' Customer response: 'You're so honest, that's great man. I will really write a review.' A detractor left as a promoter.
coaching_note: Not scored — route this to ops/estimate-accuracy review, not sales coaching. The escalation pattern here is exactly the estimate-accuracy rock in miniature and worth pulling as a case study: auto-booking quoted six hours, the confirmation call moved it to eight, the crew lead moved it to nine on site, then a third mover was added mid-move — four upward revisions, each delivered as a surprise. The customer's own diagnosis is the damaging part for the funnel: 'If it, if I been told the estimate was between 4500, I would at least shop around.' A fifth-floor elevator building at 1500 sqft is a known three-mover scenario, and Sergio said so himself; that should be caught at booking, not on the truck. One small process flag: the refund was agreed verbally with a texted receipt and no confirmation email recapping the adjusted total, which leaves no written record of the settlement.
phone_presence_notes: Absorbed a serious billing complaint without a trace of defensiveness, validated the customer's read before offering anything ('Yeah, no, a hundred percent and I appreciate you calling'), and volunteered a correction that cost the branch money — the customer ended the call unprompted with 'this is the way to run a business' and a promise to write a review.
